name: The Crusades
also_known_as: The crusades to the Holy Land, 1095–1291, with related crusades in Europe
summary: A series of wars called by popes, which promised spiritual rewards to those who fought: above all the campaigns to capture and hold Jerusalem and the Holy Land, from Urban II's call in 1095 to the fall of Acre in 1291.
place: The eastern Mediterranean (Syria, Palestine, Egypt), Constantinople, and parts of Europe

key_dates.label: First Crusade sets out; massacres of Jews in the Rhineland
Second Crusade (1147–49), preached by Bernard of Clairvaux; fails at Damascus
Saladin wins at Hattin (4 July) and takes Jerusalem (2 October)
Third Crusade (1189–92): Frederick Barbarossa, Richard I, Philip II
Richard I takes Acre and executes about 2,700 Muslim prisoners
Albigensian Crusade begins against the Cathars; massacre at Béziers
Frederick II regains Jerusalem by treaty while excommunicated
Jerusalem lost for the last time
Louis IX's crusade to Egypt (1248–54); he is captured; dies on crusade at Tunis in 1270

background.text: The Seljuk Turks had taken most of Anatolia from the Byzantine Empire after the Battle of Manzikert (1071), and Emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked the West for military help in 1095.
Pilgrimage to Jerusalem, which had been under Muslim rule since the 630s, was a central devotion of Western Christians; the church already offered remission of penance for pilgrimage.
The reforming papacy of the 11th century sought to direct the violence of the knightly class toward ends it considered holy.

happened.text: On 27 November 1095 at the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II called on Western knights to free the Eastern Christians and Jerusalem, offering full remission of penance to those who went; the crowd answered 'God wills it' (Deus vult), according to the chroniclers.
The First Crusade took Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (1099) and founded four crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch, and the County of Tripoli.
Military religious orders, the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller, were founded to protect pilgrims and defend the crusader states.

After Edessa fell (1144), the Second Crusade, led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany, failed at Damascus (1148). Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, destroyed the army of Jerusalem at Hattin in 1187 and took the city.
The Third Crusade recovered Acre and much of the coast but not Jerusalem; Richard I and Saladin agreed the Treaty of Jaffa (1192), allowing Christian pilgrims access to the city.
The Fourth Crusade, in debt to Venice, attacked the Christian city of Zara (1202) and then Constantinople, which it sacked in April 1204, setting up a Latin empire there that lasted until 1261.
Popes extended crusading to other enemies: the Cathars of southern France (from 1209), pagans in the Baltic, Muslims in Spain, and the popes' political opponents in Italy.

Later crusades to Egypt (1217–21, 1248–54) failed. Frederick II regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229, but it was lost in 1244, and the Mamluks took the last crusader strongholds, ending with Acre in 1291.

outcomes.text: The crusader states lasted almost two centuries but were lost entirely by 1291.
The sack of Constantinople in 1204 deepened the split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches; Pope John Paul II expressed regret for it to the Greek Orthodox Church in Athens in 2001.
Crusade indulgences and their financing helped develop the system of indulgences that Luther later attacked.
Crusading brought repeated violence against European Jews, and the memory of the crusades has shaped relations between Christians, Muslims, and Jews to the present day.

condemnations.reason: The Fourth Crusade excommunicated for attacking the Christian city of Zara
condemnations.status: Lifted for the French crusaders after they sought absolution; the Venetians remained excommunicated for a time

condemnations.reason: Emperor Frederick II excommunicated for delaying his crusade; he went on crusade while still excommunicated and was excommunicated again for it
condemnations.status: Lifted in 1230 (Treaty of San Germano); renewed in 1239

persecution_note: The crusades involved large-scale killing of non-combatants by crusaders and, in turn, by their Muslim opponents. The incidents below are among the best documented. Figures in medieval chronicles are often exaggerated, and modern estimates are given where possible.

persecution.title: Rhineland massacres of Jews
persecution.summary: Bands of crusaders on their way east attacked Jewish communities in Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne, and other cities, killing thousands and forcing conversions; many Jews killed themselves and their families rather than be baptized. Some bishops, such as John of Speyer, protected Jews; others could not or did not. Urban II had not called for these attacks.

responsible.name: Count Emicho of Flonheim (Leiningen)
responsible.role: Leader of the band that attacked Mainz and Worms

defended_by.name: John, Bishop of Speyer
defended_by.role: Protected Jews and punished some attackers

persecution.outcome: Thousands of Jews killed; communities destroyed.

persecution.title: Sack of Jerusalem
persecution.summary: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem, the crusaders killed many of the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. The Christian chroniclers describe a massacre, including in the area of the Temple Mount; the later Muslim historian Ibn al-Athir's figure of 70,000 is considered greatly exaggerated, and a modern estimate is about 3,000.

responsible.name: Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Toulouse, Tancred

persecution.outcome: Thousands killed; Jerusalem became the capital of the crusader kingdom.

persecution.title: Execution of captured military monks after Hattin
persecution.summary: After the Battle of Hattin, Saladin had about 200 captured Templars and Hospitallers executed and personally killed Reynald of Châtillon, who had attacked Muslim caravans and pilgrims. Saladin's later capture of Jerusalem was notably less bloody: most inhabitants were allowed to ransom themselves.

responsible.name: Saladin
responsible.role: Sultan of Egypt and Syria; ordered the executions

persecution.title: Massacres of Jews in England
persecution.summary: As England prepared for the Third Crusade, crowds attacked Jews in several towns. At York, about 150 Jews who had taken refuge in the royal castle died, many by their own hands, on 16 March 1190. Local nobles in debt to Jewish moneylenders, including Richard Malebisse, led the attack and burned the records of their debts.

responsible.name: Richard Malebisse and other indebted local nobles

persecution.outcome: Jewish communities in York and other towns destroyed; the crown fined the city but no one was executed for it.

persecution.title: Execution of Muslim prisoners at Acre
persecution.summary: After taking Acre, Richard I had about 2,700 Muslim prisoners from the garrison, with women and children according to some accounts, killed outside the city when ransom negotiations with Saladin broke down.

persecution.title: Sack of Constantinople
persecution.summary: Crusaders and Venetians stormed the Christian capital of the Byzantine Empire and plundered it for three days, killing civilians, assaulting nuns, and stripping churches, including the Hagia Sophia, of relics and treasure. Innocent III had forbidden attacks on Christians and condemned the sack, but accepted the Latin empire that followed.
persecution.outcome: The city plundered; a Latin empire ruled it until 1261.

persecution.title: Massacre at Béziers
persecution.summary: In the first major action of the crusade against the Cathars, the crusader army took Béziers and killed much of its population, Catholic and Cathar alike, in the church of the Madeleine and elsewhere. The papal legate Arnaud Amalric reported to Innocent III that about 20,000 were killed. The words 'Kill them all; God will know his own' were attributed to him by Caesarius of Heisterbach some years later, and are probably not authentic.

responsible.name: Arnaud Amalric
responsible.role: Abbot of Cîteaux and papal legate leading the crusade

persecution.outcome: Most of the town killed; the crusade continued under Simon de Montfort until 1229, followed by the Inquisition.

persecution.title: Sack of Antioch
persecution.summary: The Mamluk sultan Baybars took Antioch, one of the oldest Christian cities, killed or enslaved much of the population, and boasted of it in a letter to its absent prince, Bohemond VI.
